claims.hypothesis: The sinusoidal variations are a random fluctuation of red noise
claims.experiment: GLS tests of OVRO and Haystack data against simulated red noise matching PSD and PDF
claims.finding: The red-noise null hypothesis is rejected; a physical periodic process is present

evidence.quote: It is highly unlikely that a random process produced the observed periodicity.

claims.hypothesis: The sinusoidal variation persists in new 15 GHz data without changing the model
claims.experiment: Extrapolation of the sine fit to pre-2021 data compared with new OVRO data through 2023
claims.result: New data returned to the extrapolated sine curve in 2023
claims.finding: The constant long-term period prediction is fulfilled

evidence.loc: 2 The Continuation of the 15 GHz Sine Wave Signal in PKS 2131-021
evidence.quote: thus fulfilling the prediction, from Paper 1, of a constant long-term period

claims.hypothesis: The coherent sinusoid extends from radio to optical with a smooth phase shift
claims.experiment: Fixed-period sine fits to Haystack, OVRO, ALMA and ZTF light curves with phase relative to 15 GHz
claims.result: Phase shifts of -0.073 (91.5 GHz), -0.077 (104 GHz), -0.134 (345 GHz) and -0.352 (optical) of a cycle
claims.finding: Monotonic phase lag with frequency from 2.7 GHz to optical

evidence.loc: 6.4 Coherence of the Periodicity from the Radio to the Optical Emission
evidence.quote: The monotonic variation in phase lag with frequency from 2.7 GHz to optical frequencies demonstrates convincingly that the sinusoidal variation is caused by a physical process in the source.

claims.hypothesis: The periodicity is caused by orbital motion in a supermassive black hole binary
claims.experiment: Comparison of the multi-frequency phase shifts and amplitudes with the Kinematic Orbital model
claims.result: Data are consistent with the KO model; precessing accretion disk cannot be ruled out
claims.finding: SMBHB orbital motion is a distinct possibility but not uniquely established

evidence.quote: Of the remaining options (i) and (ii), neither can be ruled out, but it is clear that orbiting motion in an SMBHB is a distinct possibility.
